title: 11 Best Browser Automation Tools: Agents, Scripts, and Cloud Browsers
summary: Compare 11 browser automation options across AI agents, scripts, cloud browsers, and visual workflows, with pricing, capabilities, and practical tradeoffs.
body_markdown:
Browser automation tools help software navigate websites, collect information, and complete browser-based work. Options range from agents that interpret a goal to libraries that run your code to services that host the browser.


In this article, I'll go over 11 browser automation tools, their capabilities, and where I'd use each one. I'll also provide a comparison table and recommendations for different use cases.


## TL;DR


Use Case Recommendation Why


Goal-driven website tasks Browser Use Delegates navigation and interaction


Host existing agents or scripts Browser Use Managed browsers without a monthly subscription


Crawl and extract website content Firecrawl Page discovery and extraction APIs


Scripted automation and application tests Playwright Locators, assertions, and cross-browser support


Generate screenshots or PDFs Browserless Ready-made HTTP endpoints


Build spreadsheet-driven workflows visually Axiom Editable steps and integrations


## Browser Automation Basics


A browser executes JavaScript, maintains cookies, and exposes the controls a person uses. Automation becomes useful when a job depends on those capabilities: filtering a catalog, signing into a portal, downloading a report, or testing a checkout. If a supported API already provides the operation, using it may be simpler.


When comparing web browser automation tools, separate two decisions: who supplies the workflow logic and where the browser runs. A script specifies actions and conditions. An agent interprets a goal and chooses actions from the page. A visual builder represents a sequence as editable steps. Any of these approaches may use a local or managed browser.


These products can work together. Playwright can control a browser hosted by Browser Use, while an application checks the downloaded file. Headed and[headless](https://browser-use.com/posts/what-is-a-headless-browser) describe execution modes, not competing product categories. The guide to[browser agents](https://browser-use.com/posts/browser-agents) explains goal-driven control in more detail.


## 1. Browser Use


[Browser Use](https://browser-use.com/) offers affordable stealth browser hosting at[$0.02 per browser hour](https://browser-use.com/pricing) , with traffic billed separately and no required subscription. Its managed Chromium sessions include[stealth protections](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/browser/stealth) , fingerprint randomization, automatic CAPTCHA handling, and proxy support. Its AI agents operate websites from natural-language instructions, interpreting each page before choosing the next action.


The open-source Python library gives developers control over their agent implementation.[Hosted Agents](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/agent/quickstart) execute tasks through an API.[Managed browsers](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/browser/quickstart) are available independently through CDP, so you can also host an existing Playwright or Puppeteer workflow without using an agent.


Its main capabilities include:


- Goal-driven navigation, form interaction, and information collection.
- Requested output formats that your application can parse and validate.
- Sessions for continuing work and workspaces for persistent files.
- Live browser inspection and recordings for investigating execution.
- Managed Chromium sessions and proxy options for your own scripts or agents.


I'd use Browser Use for browser-based workflows such as[web scraping](https://browser-use.com/posts/web-scraping-guide-2026) , filling forms, and retrieving documents. Collecting invoices from supplier portals is one example of work across sites with different navigation and layouts. Use an agent when the steps need to adapt, or managed browsers to run existing scripts. For agent-driven workflows, account for model latency and cost, validate the result, and check whether an action completed before retrying it.


[Hosted pricing](https://browser-use.com/pricing) is model cost plus a 20% markup, with browser runtime and traffic charged separately. There is no required subscription. The open-source library has no software subscription, but you supply the model and execution resources.


## 2. Firecrawl


[Firecrawl](https://www.firecrawl.dev/) collects website content through search, scrape, and crawl APIs. It returns formats such as Markdown, HTML, and structured JSON for applications that search, analyze, or summarize web data.


Scraping retrieves a page; crawling discovers and processes multiple pages. For documentation ingestion, that can remove the need to build link discovery and content extraction yourself. Its Browser Sandbox adds interaction when reaching the information requires clicks or forms.


Capabilities include:


- Search with page-content retrieval.
- Crawling with path filters, depth limits, and asynchronous results.
- JavaScript rendering and structured extraction.
- Browser Sandbox sessions with CDP connections, live viewing, and persistent-profile options.


I would start with Firecrawl when the deliverable is website content, such as documentation for a search index or knowledge base. For submitting forms or retrieving account documents, evaluate Browser Sandbox against the interaction and session handling the workflow needs. The[Browser Use versus Firecrawl comparison](https://browser-use.com/posts/browser-use-vs-firecrawl) covers these different use cases.


The free plan includes 1,000 credits per month. Hobby provides 5,000 credits for $19 monthly, or $16 per month billed annually. Browser Sandbox code execution uses two credits per browser minute with a one-minute minimum; other endpoints have different billing rules.


## 3. Browserless


[Browserless](https://www.browserless.io/) provides remote browsers and APIs for scraping, screenshots, PDFs, and interactive automation. An existing Playwright or Puppeteer application can connect over WebSocket, while an application needing one returned artifact can use an HTTP endpoint.


The distinction matters for integration work. A screenshot service can submit a URL and receive an image. An authenticated report export generally needs a continuing session and code that navigates the account before downloading the file.


Its offering includes:


- Remote browser connections for existing scripts.
- REST endpoints for screenshots, PDFs, scraping, and content extraction.
- BrowserQL and SDK interfaces for browser operations.
- Cloud, licensed self-hosting, and private-deployment options.


I'd consider Browserless for a screenshot or PDF service where an HTTP endpoint reduces the browser code I need to maintain. For longer workflows, check that the plan's session limit covers the full job. Proxy, stealth, and CAPTCHA-handling options also have interface-specific availability and charges.


The free plan includes 1,000 units per month, two concurrent browsers, and a two-minute session limit. Prototyping is $25 per month billed annually for 20,000 units. Browser connections consume units in intervals of up to 30 seconds; additional features can increase consumption.


## 4. Browserbase


[Browserbase](https://www.browserbase.com/) hosts browsers that you can control with Playwright, Puppeteer, or Selenium. Your application creates a session through the API and connects its automation code to the remote browser.


Its open-source Stagehand SDK combines browser operations with natural-language actions and extraction. Browserbase also offers hosted Agents for prompt-driven tasks. These are separate ways to supply the workflow logic; a hosted browser alone still needs instructions from your code or agent.


Capabilities include:


- Remote browser sessions for existing automation libraries.
- Contexts for reusing cookies and browser state across sessions.
- Session replay for inspecting completed runs.
- Proxy, stealth, and CAPTCHA-handling options whose availability depends on the plan.


I would[compare Browserbase with Browser Use](https://browser-use.com/posts/browser-use-vs-browserbase) when a workflow needs managed sessions, reusable account state, and run inspection. Contexts and session replay are useful for recurring portal jobs where you need to retain access and investigate failures. Your application still needs to handle expired logins and validate the completed work.


Pricing includes a free plan with limited browser usage and paid subscriptions with included allowances and usage-based overages. Budget for browser time, proxy traffic, and any model or agent usage separately, and check concurrency and session-duration limits against the workload.


## 5. Skyvern


[Skyvern](https://www.skyvern.com/) automates recurring business processes involving websites, forms, and documents. Its hosted service and open-source self-hosting route cover tasks such as retrieving invoices, entering records, and collecting structured information from portals.


You can start a task with a prompt and URL or express the workflow through its developer interfaces. The SDK combines Playwright operations with AI methods such as` act` ,` extract` , and` validate` , allowing explicit steps and page interpretation in one workflow.


Features include:


- Structured extraction for returning fields to another application.
- Documented two-factor authentication and time-based one-time password flows.
- Browser recordings, screenshots, and execution output for inspection.
- Python and TypeScript SDKs alongside its task API.


Skyvern is worth considering for supplier-portal work where authentication and document handling are part of the process. I'd use its combination of Playwright operations and AI methods when some steps are fixed and others require interpreting the page. For a predictable sequence on a stable site, an ordinary script may be sufficient.


Plans include 5,000 one-time free credits, Hobby at $29 per month with 30,000 credits, and Pro at $149 with 150,000. Billing distinguishes AI actions, cached actions, and browser runtime, so workflow complexity affects cost.


## 6. Steel


[Steel](https://steel.dev/) offers managed browser sessions and an open-source browser server. Your agent or script supplies the interaction logic; Steel's APIs manage the browser and supporting resources, including reusable account state and downloaded files.


Each session has isolated state. Profiles carry browser data into later sessions, while file APIs handle uploads and downloads. For a daily reporting job, those resources matter as much as opening a connection: the workflow needs account access and a way to retrieve its output.


Capabilities include:


- Playwright and Puppeteer connections, with Python and Node.js session SDKs.
- Persistent profiles for cookies, settings, and account state.
- File APIs for session files and reusable storage.
- Session inspection, optional proxies/CAPTCHA solving, and a self-hosting route.


I'd consider Steel when self-hosting is a requirement or recurring jobs need reusable browser state and file handling. Its profiles and file APIs fit workflows such as downloading reports from the same accounts each day. Self-hosting adds responsibility for updates and capacity, so check which cloud features are also available in that deployment.


The Launch plan has no base fee, $30 in one-time credits, and a $0.10 browser-hour rate, rounded up to minutes. It permits ten concurrent sessions, each up to 15 minutes. Proxy traffic costs $10 per GB. Scale starts at $250 monthly plus usage, with $100 in monthly credits.


## 7. Playwright


[Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) controls Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through explicit code. It supports JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET, making it useful for both operational scripts and cross-browser application testing.


You identify elements, perform actions, and assert expected outcomes. Playwright waits for elements to be ready before acting, reducing the need for fixed sleeps. Role, label, text, and test-ID locators let you describe an element by something more meaningful than its position.


Its capabilities include:


- Isolated browser contexts and reusable authentication state.
- Trace Viewer with page snapshots, network activity, and execution history.
- Playwright Test, a JavaScript/TypeScript runner with assertions and parallel execution.
- Test generation and editor tooling for developing workflows.


Playwright is my starting point for a new checkout test suite or predictable report-export script. Its locators, assertions, and traces suit workflows where I can define the steps and expected outcomes in code. If the next action requires interpreting unfamiliar page content, a goal-driven agent may be more appropriate. For the library choice, see[Playwright vs Selenium vs Puppeteer](https://browser-use.com/posts/playwright-vs-selenium-vs-puppeteer) .


Playwright is open source. Local machines, continuous integration (CI), browser hosting, and proxies have separate costs. Its WebKit support is useful engine coverage; it doesn't establish that every behavior of the branded Safari application has been tested.


## 8. Selenium


[Selenium](https://www.selenium.dev/) is a browser automation suite centered on WebDriver. It is particularly relevant to organizations with existing test suites, multiple programming languages, or browser and operating-system combinations already supported by their testing infrastructure.


WebDriver sends commands through browser-vendor automation interfaces. Tests can use Java, Python, JavaScript, C#, or Ruby and integrate with the team's existing runner and reporting tools.


The main components are:


- WebDriver for programmatic navigation and interaction.
- Grid for distributing sessions across machines and environments.
- IDE for recording and replaying browser interactions.
- Selenium Manager for automated driver and browser management in supported setups.


I would retain Selenium when a working WebDriver suite and its integrations already meet the team's needs. Grid is useful when that suite needs to run across machines and environments. For a new JavaScript/TypeScript suite needing a bundled runner and tracing, I would evaluate Playwright first.


Selenium leaves assertions, reporting, and test orchestration to the surrounding stack. Its software is open source; Grid machines, CI workers, and commercial browser clouds still incur operating costs. A migration should solve a concrete coverage or maintenance problem before replacing an established suite.


## 9. Puppeteer


[Puppeteer](https://pptr.dev/) is a JavaScript library for controlling Chrome and Firefox from Node.js. It supplies browser APIs for navigation, interaction, inspection, and artifact generation, without requiring adoption of a complete testing framework.


It runs headless by default and can open a visible browser. Its control protocols include CDP and WebDriver BiDi; check browser support for the specific APIs your application uses.


Common capabilities include:


- Form interaction, keyboard input, navigation, and reading rendered content.
- Screenshots and PDFs for previews and report exports.
- Browser performance traces and Chrome extension automation.
- ` puppeteer-core` for applications that manage browser installation or remote connections separately.


I would use Puppeteer for a focused Node service that generates screenshots or PDF reports. The standard package downloads a compatible Chrome when its install script is permitted;` puppeteer-core` leaves browser management to the application.


For WebKit coverage or a bundled end-to-end test runner, Playwright is a better starting point. Puppeteer projects may need additional testing, reporting, and scheduling tools around the browser library. The library is open source, while browser execution, hosting, and traffic have their own costs.


## 10. Cypress


[Cypress](https://www.cypress.io/) focuses on testing applications your team owns. It supports end-to-end user journeys and component tests, with a local interface that shows commands alongside application state. Tests use JavaScript or TypeScript and run locally or in CI.


Its developer workflow is particularly useful when investigating front-end failures. For example, you can check how a checkout handles a failed payment request by controlling the network response rather than waiting for the real payment service to fail.


Capabilities include:


- Command logs and snapshots for inspecting individual steps.
- Automatic waiting and retrying assertions.
- Network interception, stubs, spies, and clocks for controlled tests.
- Optional Cloud services for recorded runs, replay, orchestration, and analytics.


I would evaluate Cypress for its debugging experience and fit with an existing release process. For general-purpose supplier-portal automation, I would start with Playwright or an agent. Cypress's execution model introduces constraints for multiple browser instances and cross-origin interactions.


The Cypress App is free and open source. Cloud and premium products have separate plans, and you provide execution capacity.


## 11. Axiom


[Axiom](https://axiom.ai/) lets you assemble browser workflows through a visual builder. Its Chrome extension represents actions such as reading a page, entering values, looping through rows, and applying conditions as configurable steps.


A typical job reads spreadsheet rows, fills a web form for each one, and writes results back. That approach can suit an operations team whose members need to edit the process themselves. A generated starting workflow still needs inspection and configuration.


Its offering includes:


- Visual browser actions, scraping, loops, and conditional logic.
- Google Sheets, Excel, Zapier, Make, and n8n integrations.
- Desktop and cloud execution, with scheduling and plan-dependent concurrency.
- Chrome, Step, and Orchestrate APIs; the code offering is labeled beta.


I'd consider Axiom when an operations team needs to build and maintain spreadsheet-driven browser workflows through editable steps. Its integrations and scheduling fit recurring data-entry and reporting jobs. For a developer-maintained workflow, compare its APIs with an established library such as Playwright before adopting the visual builder.


Pricing starts at $15 monthly for five runtime hours, with two non-renewing trial hours. Pro costs $50 monthly for 30 hours and adds integrations/API features. Check the desktop/cloud entitlements for the intended workflow.


## Choosing a Browser Automation Tool


- If you do **routine tasks or app testing** : use scripted automation.
- If you do **tasks across unfamiliar sites** : consider an AI agent.
- If you do **automation without writing code** : use a visual workflow builder.


## Browser Automation Costs


Compare cost per completed task, including browser runtime, model usage, proxy traffic, and hosting or subscription fees. Retries, idle time, and minimum billing increments can make the total higher than the headline rate.

## My Recommendations


I would start with Browser Use for goal-driven website tasks or hosting an existing agent or script. For predictable workflows and new application test suites, Playwright is my default; established Selenium or Cypress suites need a concrete reason to migrate.


For content ingestion, evaluate Firecrawl before building page discovery yourself. Browserless suits ready-made screenshot/PDF operations, Steel offers a self-hostable browser-server option, and Axiom provides visual authoring. Pilot the shortlisted tool on a representative task and verify the result outside the automation tool.
